A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Medix research despite the changed title and publication format. Their main text, equations, figures, tables and Appendices A–C are readable and support a reliable comparison.

before.justification: v1 reports original Medix benchmark results, a synthetic outlier-extraction experiment, ablations and computational profiling in the main text and appendices.

after.justification: v2 retains those empirical results and adds ResNet-50, ImageNet-1k and filtering-control experiments in Appendices A.8–A.10.

M1.justification: Algorithm 1 changes its loop condition from OR to AND between the iteration-limit and deviation conditions, allowing either stopping condition to terminate filtering. This is a limited correction to the reported procedure; the gradient-based greedy extraction and subsequent binary-detector training remain substantively the same.

E1.justification: Appendix A.9 adds ImageNet-1k as an InD dataset, evaluated against SVHN and TEXTURES at 224×224 resolution. This substantially extends coverage beyond the retained CIFAR, synthetic-data and unseen-OOD experiments to high-resolution, thousand-class recognition.

E2.justification: Appendix A.10 introduces and evaluates MSP-filter + binary, which replaces median filtering with MSP-based candidate selection while retaining Medix's second-stage detector. Existing comparator sets are retained; the additional WOODS evaluations extend an existing comparator to new settings.

E3.justification: The added experiments introduce ResNet-50 evaluations with reported gradient dimension 2048, ImageNet testing at 224×224 resolution, and a controlled comparison holding second-stage training fixed while changing the filter. These substantially expand the evaluation design; the original CIFAR splits, training budgets, hyperparameters and metrics remain unchanged.

E4.justification: Appendix A.10 adds a direct test of whether performance comes from median filtering or merely the two-stage pipeline. Appendix A.8 tests robustness to larger gradient dimensionality, and Figures 6–7 add gradient-distribution diagnostics for CIFAR-10 and ImageNet-1k. The earlier median comparison, hyperparameter and pseudo-label analyses are retained.

E5.justification: Tables 1, 2 and 4 retain their five-run averaging statements and existing uncertainty entries. The new evaluations introduce no specified seed counts, confidence intervals, significance tests or new uncertainty-estimation procedures.

E6.justification: Numerical results in Tables 1–6 are unchanged. Tables 7–8 add ResNet-50 and ImageNet results, and Table 9 adds MSP-filter + binary results while redisplaying existing scores. The new ImageNet/TEXTURES comparison reports Medix FPR95/AUROC of 7.53/97.98 versus WOODS 5.43/98.89, establishing an exception to uniform superiority.

T1.justification: Section 4 and Appendix C substantially replace the theoretical setup and proofs with an ideal size-constrained filter, random mixture counts, explicit reference-accuracy assumptions and revised concentration bounds. The inlier contamination term changes from pi/[2(1-pi)] to pi/(1-pi). The earlier fourth-moment inlier-error theorem is replaced by Corollary 4.5 on reference-median accuracy, with different reasoning and a narrower conclusion.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction and conclusion retain the central claims of median-based outlier extraction, theoretical error guarantees and superior empirical performance against competitive baselines. The shortened contribution bullets and new title do not redefine these headline contributions. The abstract still claims outperformance 'across the board.'

C2.justification: Remark 4.6 explicitly limits the guarantees to the ideal optimizer and distinguishes them from empirical support for greedy Algorithm 1. The revised theory interprets inlier error through displacement and mixture-count fluctuations. New discussions address dimensional scalability, acknowledge WOODS's ImageNet/TEXTURES advantage, and attribute the filtering-control performance gap to candidate-set contamination.

D1.justification: v2 adds an explicit Medix code hyperlink, a WOODS implementation link and Appendix A.11 specifying sample-axis mean/median operations with PyTorch dim=0 examples. Existing training and hardware details remain, while v1's explicit sigmoid-surrogate explanation in Section 3.2 is omitted; no replacement loss is established.

R1.justification: Section 6 adds positioning against generation-based OOD approaches, including new citations to OODGAN, GOOD, HybOOD and diffusion-based methods. It discusses their usefulness when wild data is unavailable and leaves direct comparison to future work. The Wilk–Gnanadesikan reference is removed; publication updates and duplicate-reference cleanup do not change comparator identity.

P1.justification: The theoretical exposition and Appendix C are extensively rewritten and reorganized into explicit setup, assumptions, scoped statements and compact proofs. v2 also retitles the paper, condenses introductory contributions, expands the experimental roadmap and adds explanatory appendix subsections. This exceeds localized language editing.

P2.justification: v2 adds an overview diagram, three experimental tables and two gradient-diagnostic figures, and substantially revises the notation table. Existing figures are retained with relocation, resizing and renumbering. Journal formatting also changes typography, headers, theorem boxes and page layout throughout.

improvement.justification: The revised theory substantially improves precision by replacing v1's swapping arguments with explicit size constraints, mixture-count reasoning and clearly scoped guarantees. The controlled filtering comparison and larger-scale evaluations address important attribution and scalability gaps. These gains outweigh remaining shortcomings: the guarantees are narrower and do not cover the greedy solver, while the unchanged 'across the board' claim conflicts with the new ImageNet/TEXTURES results.
